thread.title: Animal Stories…

author: View all posts by Jordan B Jolley
title: Animal Stories…
text:
Last week I published a fable that was at least two years in the making. Even though it was a shorter story, it turned out to be challenging to develop. From the get-go, I wanted to have the theme be about the fragility of human society engrained in a tale about nonhuman animals.
My animal subjects were initially rabbits, given their social behaviors, but I had trouble deciding whether these rabbits, and other animals in my fable, would be fully anthropomorphized, or if their fate would be determined by the downfall of a human civilization. I really struggled with the indecision here. I would write a few pages of the anthropomorphic version only to change my mind and have them more like actual rabbits among humans. That’s the curse of O.C.D., which I clinically suffer from.
The developing story gradually evolved to eastern-inspiration, particularly the Ind0chinese region. It was here in my research that I read a little about the Medieval Khmer city of Angkor. What really impressed me was the complex infrastructure the city had to provide food and wealth, only to have it come crashing down by 1431 after being sacked by the Siamese-Ayutthaya army. Many historians believed Angkor had already been in decline by then due to climate change that compromised their canal systems. With these different factors contributing to the dissolution of a once prosperous civilization, it provided the perfect material for me to incorporate thematically into my story.
When I decided to set my story in a city inspired by Angkor, I decided to change the main animal characters from a warren of rabbits to a clan of dholes: a kind of wild dog not unlike a wolf. I eventually wanted the animals to be predators by nature, the so-called brutes of the jungle. Rudyard Kipling’s story “Red Dog” also motivated me to use dholes to offer a counterpoint to their villainous portrayal in “The Second Jungle Book”. It also helped that dholes have sophisticated hunting tactics, cute pre-hunting rituals to encourage one another, and their rather gruesome way of devouring their prey while it’s still alive. I wanted to show that even though they are gruesome, they must feast this way to survive. They aren’t evil creatures for this reason.
I’ve come across many animal tales, some of them new and published online. However, there’s a common thing in these stories that heavily imply that real animals are neither sentient nor capable of thought, something I vehemently disagree with. After reading these stories, I’d come to decide that I didn’t want my dholes to be fully anthropomorphic. Sure, they still speak to humans and other animals, but aside from that, they behave just like real dholes. It’s come to the point that should I write more animals fables in the future (and I most definitely will), I want to give them as many realistic traits as possible however much the plot will allow. I’ve already written a story with fully anthropomorphic animals (“Our Cry”), and even then the dogs and jackals in that fable have dog-isms associated with them. The fact is, I love animals; all species. I have a deep spiritual connection with the earth and life, and I have a profound connection with animals. I believe they have spirits, and I know they are sentient. They think differently from humans, not less than. Just because they are not industrious as we are, doesn’t mean they’re less evolved. Each species evolves in its own direction. Even if thousands of years pass, most animals will not be any more human than they are now. They evolve for their own means of mortal existence.
Okay, I rambled quite a bit there, but I had to get that off my chest. To put it simply, if I’m to portray animals in my stories, whether fully anthropomorphic, partially anthropomorphic, or not anthropomorphic at all, I want to have a good reason why I am displaying the animals the way I do. In the end, I feel like “No Place” is the best version of the story I had been developing for so long, and I’m glad it’s finished. My biggest wish now is to have people read it and enjoy it. It’s now available on Amazon Kindle and Patreon.
To close, I want to quickly talk about my fable’s title. It does connect with the story, but I want you to find out how for yourself. The reason why I ultimately chose this title is because in ancient Greek, “no place” translates to “utopia”. For most of us, when we think of utopia, we think of an idealistic place. The name actually comes from Thomas Moore’s book “Utopia”. The reason why he used this name for his ideal city is because it doesn’t actually exist. “The perfect place” doesn’t exist on earth, at least not yet; that is why it is currently in the state of being “no place”.
Thanks for reading this and I hope you decide to read the story now.
–
